cf.title: Refactor pgbench - pure mechanical modularization into 10 module pairs (stats, variable, poller, random, expr, script, commands, init, engine, report)

input.subject: [PATCH] Refactor pgbench to make future improvements easier

verdict_reasoning: The surviving objections demand-1 and maintenance-fit-1 both fail level 1b. The split has no user-visible effect, and the only named consumer is the author's own later work, which message #12 still lists as a follow-up. Messages #13 and #14 ask to start from one feature with only the refactoring it needs, and the thread has no answer to that yet. The goal may be fine, but the list has to agree on the approach before code review makes sense.

brief.title: Split pgbench.c into ten modules by pure code movement
brief.problem: pgbench.c is a single file of about 8,000 lines that mixes statistics, variables, polling, script parsing, meta-commands, initialization and the client state machine. The author says this makes later pgbench work harder, in particular his planned contrib/pgbench extension and features for TPC-like workloads. Reviewers found the motivation weak without a concrete feature that needs the split.
brief.proposed_design: v7 moves code out of pgbench.c into ten module pairs: stats, variable, poller, random, expr, script, commands, init, engine and report. The author states that function bodies and signatures stay identical; the only changes are dropping static on cross-file functions and globals, adding extern declarations, and moving two static inline timing helpers to stats.h. After the series pgbench.c keeps about 930 lines for option globals, usage() and main().
author_claims: All 136 function definitions keep identical bodies, parameter lists and return types at every commit 0001 to 0010.
Remaining code in pgbench.c is not reordered; each diff is only include updates, static removals and block deletions.
Earlier versions built with Make and Meson and passed all 686 pgbench TAP tests.
The split prepares moving random distributions, hashing and permute into src/common and exposing them in SQL through contrib/pgbench.
brief.thread_state: Zsolt Parragi and Koshi Shibagaki asked for move-only patches; Parragi found v6 0004 still reordered pgbench.c, and v7 claims to fix this. Dmitry Dolgov and Shibagaki then asked to drop the split-only approach and start from one feature, such as the distribution generators, with only the refactoring it needs.
unclear: The material has commit messages only for 0001 to 0008; 0009 and 0010 prose is missing.
No one has yet confirmed that v7 is move-only; the invariants are the author's own claims.
The author has not said how the split affects back-patching of pgbench fixes to older branches.
The promised design document or table of which function goes to which module is not in the thread.
The author has not said which concrete feature needs this module layout.

objections.title: No concrete feature or user shown to need this module layout
objections.failure_scenario: After the split is committed, every open pgbench patch must be rebased onto ten new files, and each back-patched pgbench fix must be adapted by hand. If the feature that motivated the split never lands, or needs different boundaries, the project pays that cost and may move the code a second time.
objections.argument: The only stated beneficiary is the author's own planned work: contrib/pgbench and TPC-like features (messages #3, #12). No other user or developer asks for the split. Dolgov calls the motivation weak and asks for one feature with only the refactoring it needs (message #13); Shibagaki withdraws support for split-only review for the same reason (message #14). Message #12 says the split helps "anyone wanting to improve pgbench" but names no such person or patch, and that argument would fit any large source file.
objections.author_must_show: Which concrete pgbench feature, wanted by someone besides the author, cannot reasonably be built on today's pgbench.c, and which of the ten modules does it need?

precedents.title: Docs: make source file path references consistent

critic.reasoning: Messages #13 and #14 ask for one feature with only the refactoring it needs, and message #12 names that feature only as a follow-up. Shibagaki's earlier interest in the refactoring is the one sign of wider demand, and message #14 makes it conditional on a concrete use case.

objections.title: Module boundaries chosen before any feature that would use them
objections.failure_scenario: The split goes in, then the planned distribution or contrib/pgbench work needs random.c in src/common and a different expr/commands interface. A second large reshuffle follows. Back-branch fixes and git blame in pgbench pay for both rounds.
objections.argument: v7 makes about 66 functions and many globals external, including throttle_delay, timer_exceeded, use_quiet and scale, without any encapsulation. The new files are therefore coupled through shared globals, so the split adds files but not real interfaces. Messages #13 and #14 ask for one feature first, so that the boundaries are judged against a real consumer. Message #12 still names that feature only as a later follow-up.
objections.author_must_show: Which part of the distribution-generator or contrib/pgbench work needs exactly this ten-module layout, and would random.c move again for it?

critic.reasoning: The v7 commit messages confirm that the split exports globals such as throttle_delay, timer_exceeded, use_quiet and scale unchanged. Messages #1 and #6 plan to move the random code to src/common, so a second move of random.c is the author's own stated next step.

refuted.title: Split has no feature that needs it; earlier refactor-only steps stalled for this
refuted.failure_scenario: A committer pushes the ten-module split. Every open pgbench patch, and every fix later back-patched to branches that still have the single pgbench.c, must be rebased or hand-ported. If the contrib/pgbench and distribution work is later reshaped or dropped, the project carries this churn and the module layout without the feature it was built for.
refuted.argument: Messages #13 and #14 ask to start from one feature, such as the distribution generators, and limit the refactoring to what that feature needs. The v7 cover letter in message #12 promises that follow-up but does not answer this request. [P2] stopped for a similar reason: reviewers wanted a plan showing how the step reached its stated goal. [P4] shows that a cleanup can lose on cost against value when no user-facing gain follows from it.
refuted.author_must_show: Which concrete feature, for example SQL-callable distribution generators, needs these ten module boundaries, and which of the ten splits could it do without?

precedents.title: Split StdRdOptions into HeapOptions and ToastOptions
Docs: make source file path references consistent

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of demand-1, which makes the same point from messages #13 and #14 without leaning on precedents. [P2] was returned for not going far enough and [P4] is a documentation cleanup, so neither shows that an earlier split-only step stalled for this reason.

refuted.title: Every back-patched pgbench fix must be hand-ported across the split
refuted.failure_scenario: A committer fixes a bug in advanceConnectionState on master, where it now lives in engine.c. On the supported branches the same code is still in pgbench.c, so the patch does not apply. For about five years each fix needs a separate, manually checked port, and git blame for older code goes through a large move commit.
refuted.argument: Message #2 counts about four back-patched pgbench commits per year and judges that acceptable. The proposal itself does not weigh this cost against a gain, and per message #13 the gain is only smaller files. A committer would likely accept the porting cost for a split that a feature needs, and less likely for a split done on its own.
refuted.author_must_show: What concrete gain for later pgbench work outweighs several years of manual ports of back-patched fixes into the ten new files?

critic.reasoning: Message #2 measured the cost at about four back-patched pgbench commits per year and judged it acceptable, and no one in the thread disputed that. The remaining point, that no gain is shown to justify the cost, is the same as demand-1.

touch_points.label: backpatchability
touch_points.reason: Fixes to code moved out of pgbench.c need manual ports to older branches; message #2 counts about four such commits per year.

touch_points.label: maintenance burden ("who maintains this in 10 years")
touch_points.reason: The series adds ten module pairs and makes about 66 functions and many globals external inside src/bin/pgbench.

touch_points.label: doesn't fit what Postgres is about (extension / external tool / already solved)

questions: Which concrete pgbench feature needs these module boundaries, and which of the ten modules does that feature use?
Does anyone besides the author have a pgbench patch or plan that today's single pgbench.c blocks or makes harder?
Will random.c move again to src/common for the contrib/pgbench work, and if so, why not move it there in one step?
Can the series be reduced to the distribution-generator feature plus only the code moves it needs, as messages #13 and #14 ask?
Where is the promised table of which function goes to which module, and what do patches 0009 and 0010 move?

committability.owner_note: A committer who knows pgbench and its back-branch history would have to own it. The material shows reviewers in the thread but does not identify any of them as a committer.
committability.liability: The owner signs for a move-only claim across about 7,000 moved lines, and for manual ports of pgbench fixes to older branches for about five years.
committability.author_follow_up: The author answered reviews and posted reworked versions up to v7 within a month, and plans follow-up work on top of the split.

not_now.evidence_that_would_change_it: A posted feature patch, such as SQL-callable distribution generators, that uses specific module boundaries from this series, or pgbench patches from other developers that the single file demonstrably hinders.

priority.reason: The split changes nothing for users and its only named consumer is unposted follow-up work, while verifying about 7,000 moved lines as move-only is costly. Reviewers in messages #13 and #14 ask for a feature-first series with only the refactoring that feature needs.

provisional_note: No one has confirmed that v7 is move-only; that claim and the amount of coupling through exported globals need the code. The commit messages for 0009 and 0010 were not in the material.
disclosure: Prepared by an AI harness; treat as a devil's advocate, not a verdict.

precedents_retrieved.title: pgbench - add random_zipfian function
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch adds a random_zipfian(min, max, s) function to pgbench, so that skewed, YCSB-like workloads can be run without YCSB. It uses a per-thread cache of harmonic numbers for s < 1 and a rejection method for s > 1.
precedents_retrieved.objection: In message #47 Daniel Gustafsson returned the patch in the 2017-09 commitfest because it was Waiting for author and no new version came during that commitfest. The author later posted new versions, Fabien COELHO marked it ready for committer, and Teodor Sigaev reported it pushed on 2017-12-14. No visible message explains the 2018-06-26 decision.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: Since this patch has been Waiting for author and no update on this patch has been posted during the commitfest, it is Returned with feedback.

precedents_retrieved.title: Split StdRdOptions into HeapOptions and ToastOptions
precedents_retrieved.objectors: Michael Paquier, Georgios Kokolatos, Jeff Davis
precedents_retrieved.summary: Replace the single StdRdOptions structure used to store relation options with separate HeapOptions and ToastOptions structures, with matching per-relkind option-fetching macros and asserts. This was presented as the last step of a larger effort to split reloptions per relkind and access method before moving option definitions into AM code.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Reviewers considered the patch a step in the right direction but not far enough: they wanted table-AM-specific reloption handling (heap options defined in the heap AM handler, as is done for index AMs), and Jeff Davis asked for a plan showing how this would lead there. The patch then stopped applying to HEAD; the author's last message says the rebase needed careful work and would come after his vacation, and no newer version appears in the visible messages before the entry was returned with feedback.

precedents_retrieved.title: Split index and table statistics into different types of stats
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch splits the cumulative statistics kind PGSTAT_KIND_RELATION into PGSTAT_KIND_TABLE and a new PGSTAT_KIND_INDEX, with index-specific counting macros and SQL-callable functions. The goal is sensible field names for index stats and lower memory use, since index entries currently carry unused table counters.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The patch stalled. Review comments from Andres Freund and Melanie Plageman were still open, and the author put the work on hold until the related "Generate pg_stat_get_xact*() functions with Macros" patch was done. After that patch was committed, no new version came; the CFM returned the entry because it no longer applied and tests failed.

precedents_retrieved.title: Docs: make source file path references consistent
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch makes documentation references to .h and .c files in the source tree consistent. It uses the full source-tree path when the text points to a file's location, and the short relative path, as in #include directives, when the text refers to including a header.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Tom Lane questioned whether the change was worth the time, since reaching and keeping full consistency costs more than it gives. Andres Freund added that every patch costs reviewers time to read, which has to be weighed against its benefit. The author agreed and withdrew the patch.

precedents_retrieved.title: Split index and table statistics into different types of stats
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch splits the cumulative statistics for indexes and tables into two kinds, PGSTAT_KIND_TABLE and a new PGSTAT_KIND_INDEX, with index-specific counting macros and SQL functions. The goal is sensible field names and lower memory use, since index stats today reuse the table format and leave many fields unused.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Andres Freund objected that the patch makes bufmgr.c aware of the relation kind, and suggested first moving relkind-agnostic counters such as blocks_hit and blocks_fetched into per-relfilenode stats. The author agreed to do the relfilenode stats work first and set the entry to Waiting on Author. Michael Paquier later returned the entry because there was no update since January 2024 and the relfilenode work had been posted separately.

precedents_retrieved.title: array_random
precedents_retrieved.objectors: Dean Rasheed, Aleksander Alekseev, Tom Lane
precedents_retrieved.summary: Add a core function array_random(min, max, dims [, lbounds]) for int4, int8 and numeric that returns an array of the given dimensions filled with random values in [min, max]. The author argued that it does more than array_fill and is faster and easier than building a multi-dimensional array in PL/pgSQL.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Reviewers saw no field demand to justify the added C code, since filling a 1-D array with random values is easy in SQL or plpgsql. Aleksander Alekseev objected that the function both generates values and shapes the array, and suggested a separate reshape function. Tom Lane and Dean Rasheed agreed that a reshape function would be more useful but questioned whether anyone needs it; the entry was then withdrawn.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
There's an infinite amount of stuff that would be faster if coded
in C than if written in SQL or plpgsql.  We can't support it all,
so we need some fairly high bar to accepting what functionality
we'll support.

precedents_retrieved.title: Introduce some randomness to autovacuum
precedents_retrieved.objectors: Sami Imseih, Robert Treat, David Rowley
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch rotates the list of tables autovacuum collects in each database by a random offset, so a different table is vacuumed first each round and spinning on one table or starvation of others is reduced. A later version put this behind a GUC that selects a vacuum strategy, and v2-0002 skipped tables whose last autovacuum removed few dead tuples.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Reviewers held that randomness hides the problem and makes autovacuum scheduling, already complex, nondeterministic. Sami Imseih argued that users can already handle both cases: disable autovacuum on a failing table, and change autovacuum_max_workers online for starvation. David Rowley proposed fixing the root cause instead, by not revisiting a table until its OldestXmin cutoff has moved forward. The visible thread ends in May 2025 after v2 was posted, and no closing message is shown.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: I will argue that for the two cases that this proposal is seeking to correct, we already have good solutions that could be implemented by a user.

precedents_retrieved.title: Add WAL recovery info such as current WAL file and WAL source to server logs
precedents_retrieved.objectors: Robert Haas, Nathan Bossart, Michael Paquier
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch logs which WAL segment recovery is processing and where it came from (archive, stream), so cloud users who cannot see the ps display can follow recovery in the server log. Later versions add a log_wal_traffic GUC (none, medium, high) to control how often these messages appear.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Early reviewers objected that per-segment LOG messages make the logs too noisy on busy systems. Robert Haas then said the log_wal_traffic design overlaps with log_startup_progress_interval, which reports by elapsed time and so also shows when replay is stalled, and asked that the existing facility be extended instead. The author reworked the patch on that basis as v10, but the visible messages do not show why the entry was then withdrawn.

roaster_notes.note: Back-patching cost is not raised separately, because message #2 estimates about four back-patched pgbench commits per year and calls that manageable. The thread also points to an earlier proposal, CF 7225 for contrib/pgbench (messages #3 and #14). Its outcome is not in the material.

From the standards and compatibility angle the series changes nothing users see: no SQL syntax, GUCs, pgbench options, script language, output formats or dump behaviour. Back-patching was raised in message #2, where the reviewer judged about four back-patched pgbench commits a year to be manageable. Whether v7 is really move-only needs the code and is outside this angle.

The series moves code inside the pgbench client binary and adds no persistent or cross-node state: no on-disk format, WAL, catalog, wire protocol or server ABI change. The cost of back-patching pgbench fixes was raised and judged acceptable in message #2, at about four back-patched commits per year.

v7 is a move-only split of the pgbench client source. It adds no option, no SQL object, no server-side code and no default. It does not touch privileges, authentication or what a user can see. Removing static on symbols inside one client binary does not expose anything to other users. The later contrib/pgbench extension would need its own security review, but it is not part of this proposal.
No hot-path, catalog or external-dependency cost: the change is limited to the pgbench client binary.

v7 is a move-only split of pgbench.c with no user-visible behaviour, so no existing feature, contrib module or extension does the same job. The later goal of exposing pgbench distributions in SQL is not part of v7, and I cannot name an existing extension that reliably provides them, so nothing is raised from this angle.

One demand objection only. The split has no direct user-visible effect, so demand has to come from a feature built on top of it, and none is shown yet. The suggestion in message #14 to start from the distribution generators would supply that.
